# Anticipation

The audience sees a small move the **opposite way** first: a crouch before a jump, a wind-up before a throw. That move is called **anticipation**.

![A marker moves a short way back, then travels in a big arc forward](asset:anticipation)

It does two jobs. Bodies really do load up before they move. And it shows the audience where to look just before the big move.

Squash and stretch and anticipation are two of the "twelve principles of animation." Two Disney animators, Frank Thomas and Ollie Johnston, wrote them down in 1981, but a whole studio had worked them out in the 1930s. Its large ink-and-paint staff, mostly women, put every drawing on screen, and their names never appeared there.

{{deeper}}

**Leave anticipation out** and the audience can miss the leap, because nothing told them where to look.

**Who worked the principles out.** From 1932 the Disney studio ran drawing and "action analysis" classes led by Don Graham, an art teacher from the Chouinard Art Institute. Animators also taught each other: in a 1935 memo Walt Disney credited talks by Norm Ferguson, Fred Moore, Ham Luske and Fred Spencer. The inkers and painters put every one of those drawings onto cels, the clear sheets that were filmed.

**One thing that is not anticipation.** The pause at the top of the ball's hop can look like a moment of getting ready. It is not anticipation. It is the ease from the spacing lesson: the ball slowing into the top and out of it.
